description: Zero-knowledge proofs let you convince someone a statement is true without revealing WHY. Apply this to mathematics: a zero-knowledge proof of a theorem T convinces the verifier that T is provable in PA without revealing any step of the proof. Conjecture: Every theorem provable in Peano Arithmetic has a zero-knowledge proof whose communication complexity is polynomial in the length of the theorem statement (not the proof). This follows from the PCP theorem combined with the fact that PA-proofs can be arithmetized. The zero-knowledge protocol: (1) Prover commits to each proof step using a collision-resistant hash. (2) Verifier randomly challenges one proof step. (3) Prover opens that step and shows it follows from the axioms. Repeating O(k) times gives soundness error 2^{-k}. The proof is zero-knowledge because the verifier only sees one random step per challenge. Test: implement a zero-knowledge proof system for propositional tautologies and prove that a verifier learns nothing beyond the validity of the tautology. Impact: mathematicians can certify results without revealing their methods — a mathematical equivalent of sealed-bid auctions for proof strategies.
proof_strategy: Arithmetize PA-proofs: encode each proof step as a polynomial equation over a finite field F_p. Apply the PCP theorem: every NP statement has a probabilistically checkable proof of constant query complexity. Convert the PCP to zero-knowledge using the Fiat-Shamir heuristic: the prover commits to the PCP oracle, the verifier sends a random challenge, and the prover responds with a proof that is zero-knowledge by the hiding property of the commitment. Prove soundness: a cheating prover must fool the verifier with probability at most 2^{-k}. Prove zero-knowledge: the simulator can generate indistinguishable transcripts without the proof. Test: implement for propositional resolution proofs of length up to 1000.
title: Zero-Knowledge Theorem Proving: I Can Prove Fermat's Last Theorem Without Showing You the Proof

description: Gödel showed self-reference breaks completeness, but what if self-referential proofs are not paradoxes but VALID mathematical objects? Develop a proof theory where proofs can reference their own structure — a proof of theorem T can contain a subproof that assumes T as a hypothesis, forming a circular dependency that is resolved through a fixed-point construction. Conjecture: Non-well-founded proofs form a convergent fixed point under a natural topolog: the space of proof trees with the tree topology is a Scott domain, and self-referential proofs correspond to infinite chains whose lub is a valid proof. A proof that references itself is like a recursive function: it converges if the self-reference occurs at a strictly smaller ordinal. Test: formalize non-well-founded proof trees as coinductive types in Lean 4, prove that the proof of 'P implies P' by assuming P is a valid non-well-founded proof with ordinal height 1, and show that the liar sentence 'this statement is unprovable' is NOT a valid non-well-founded proof because its ordinal height is undefined. Impact: turns the liar paradox from a bug into a feature — self-referential proofs are a new class of mathematical object with their own consistency conditions.
proof_strategy: Define NWFP (non-well-founded proofs) as coinductive types: a proof is a tree where children are proofs, but cycles are allowed as long as each cycle has decreasing ordinal rank. Define ordinal height: oh(P) = sup{oh(Q)+1 : Q is a subproof of P}. A NWFP is valid if oh(P) is a well-defined ordinal. Prove consistency: if NWFP proves False, then oh(False) < oh(False), contradiction. Prove completeness: every true Pi_1 sentence has a NWFP of finite height. Test: formalize in Lean 4 and verify the P-implies-P example.
title: Non-Well-Founded Proofs: Proofs That Reference Themselves

description: The integers Z live on a line, but what happens to arithmetic on a curved space? Define hyperbolic integers Z_H as the set of points in the Poincaré disk that are images of Z under a discrete subgroup Gamma of PSL(2,R). Define hyperbolic primes as the vertices of the tessellation induced by Gamma, and hyperbolic addition/multiplication via the group action. Conjecture: Z_H has unique factorization into hyperbolic primes, and the hyperbolic prime number theorem holds: the number of hyperbolic primes in a hyperbolic disk of radius R is asymptotic to R^2 / (2 log R). The hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum_{n in Z_H, |n|_H > 0} 1/|n|_H^{2s} satisfies a functional equation and has zeros only on the critical line Re(s) = 1/2. Test: compute zeta_H(s) for the modular group Gamma = PSL(2,Z) and verify that the first 100 zeros lie on Re(s) = 1/2. Impact: number theory on curved spaces — where primes are geometric objects and the Riemann Hypothesis might be PROVABLE.
proof_strategy: Define Z_H as the orbit of 0 under Gamma = PSL(2,Z) acting on the Poincaré disk. Define |n|_H as the hyperbolic distance from the origin. Prove Z_H is a discrete subset of the disk. Define the hyperbolic zeta function zeta_H(s) = sum 1/|n|_H^{2s} and prove it converges for Re(s) > 1. Prove the functional equation zeta_H(s) = pi^{s-1/2} Gamma((1-s)/2)/Gamma(s/2) zeta_H(1-s) using Selberg's trace formula. Test: compute first 100 zeros numerically and verify Re(s) = 1/2.
title: Hyperbolic Number Theory: Arithmetic on the Poincaré Disk

description: Conway's surreal numbers are the largest ordered field, containing every real number and infinitely many infinities and infinitesimals. But what if a surreal number could be in SUPERPOSITION — simultaneously equal to multiple values until observed? Define quantum surreal numbers as surreal-valued quantum states: |psi> = sum_i alpha_i |No_i> where No_i are surreal numbers and alpha_i are complex amplitudes. Conjecture: The quantum surreal field Q(No) is a non-Archimedean quantum field where the spectral theorem extends: every self-adjoint operator on a quantum surreal Hilbert space has a spectral decomposition into surreal-valued projections. The key insight is that infinitesimal surreal numbers provide a natural framework for quantum measurement: the probability of observing |No_i> is not alpha_i^2 (which may be infinitesimal) but the standard part of alpha_i^2. Test: construct the quantum surreal number |psi> = (1/sqrt(2))|0> + (1/sqrt(2))|epsilon> where epsilon is an infinitesimal surreal, and prove that measuring |psi> gives 0 with probability st(1/2) = 1/2 and epsilon with probability st(1/2 * epsilon^2) = 0 — the infinitesimal is unobservable! Impact: a mathematical framework where quantum mechanics and non-Archimedean analysis meet, giving infinitesimal probabilities a rigorous treatment.
proof_strategy: Define Q(No) as the tensor product of the surreal field No with the complex numbers C. Define quantum surreal Hilbert space H_Q(No) as the completion of Q(No)^n with respect to the surreal-valued inner product. Prove the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators on H_Q(No) by transfinite induction on the birthday of the surreal eigenvalues. The key lemma: if A is self-adjoint with surreal eigenvalues, then A = integral lambda dE(lambda) where E(lambda) are projections and lambda ranges over surreal numbers up to the birthday of A. Test: construct the 2x2 example and verify measurement probabilities.
title: Quantum Surreal Numbers: Superposition of All Real Numbers

description: Borges' Library of Babel contains every possible 410-page book — approximately 25^{1312000} volumes. The library is finite but vast beyond comprehension. Formalize the Library as the set of all strings over a 25-symbol alphabet of length 1312000. Conjecture: The probability that a random volume contains a meaningful proof of a given theorem T is approximately |T| * 25^{-k} where |T| is the length of T and k is the proof complexity of T. Moreover, the Library contains a universal catalog — a single volume that encodes the location of every other volume — and this catalog can be found in polynomial time using a variant of the de Bruijn sequence construction. The deepest question: does the Library contain its own complete catalog? By a diagonal argument, no single volume can encode all volumes (since 25^{1312000} > 1312000 * log_2(25^{1312000})). But a DISTRIBUTED catalog spanning N volumes can encode the entire Library if N > 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_2(25)). Test: compute the exact probability of finding a valid Lean 4 proof of a specific theorem in the Library. Construct a de Bruijn-based catalog for a mini-Library with alphabet size 4 and book length 16. Impact: the mathematics of universal information spaces — every possible text exists, but finding meaning requires a guide.
proof_strategy: Define B = {0,...,24}^{1312000} as the Library. Compute |B| = 25^{1312000}. Define the meaning probability P(T) = sum_{b in B: b contains proof of T} 1/|B|. Prove P(T) >= |T| * 25^{-k(T)} where k(T) is the Kolmogorov complexity of T. Construct a distributed catalog using de Bruijn sequences: encode each volume's address as a substring of a de Bruijn sequence B(25, m) for m = ceil(log_{25}(1312000)). Prove the catalog requires N >= 25^{1312000} / (1312000 * log_{25}(2)) volumes. Test: implement the mini-Library with alphabet 4, book length 16, and compute meaning probabilities.
title: The Library of Babel: Combinatorics of the Universal Library

description: Conjecture that for any set of N points on a d‑dimensional smooth submanifold of ℝ^M and any mapping Φ with Kruskal rank at least d+1, the number of dichotomies C_F(N) realizable by linear separators in the image space satisfies C_F(N) ≤ ∑_{i=0}^{d} binomial(N-1, i), which is strictly tighter than the classical Cover bound when d < M.

description:
For every simple graph G with maximum degree Δ, any number of agents ℓ ≥ 2Δ is sufficient to guarantee a stochastic‑dominance envy‑free‐up‑to‑one‑item (SD‑EF1) allocation of the vertices on the agents, and moreover there exists a deterministic polynomial‑time algorithm that produces such an allocation.  This conjecture sharpens the currently known existential and algorithmic bounds of ℓ ≥ 3Δ−1 (and ℓ ≥ (3+ε)Δ) by reducing the required number of agents to 2Δ.

In graph‑theoretic terms the conjecture asserts that every Δ‑bounded simple graph admits a proper vertex‑colouring with at most 2Δ colours in which each colour class can be mapped to an agent in such a way that the resulting allocation satisfies the SD‑EF1 condition for any common preference order.  The conjecture is falsifiable: a single counter‑example graph with Δ and ℓ < 2Δ that admits no SD‑EF1 allocation would refute it.

This conjecture is formalizable in Lean 4 as a statement about the existence of a partition of V(G) into ℓ independent sets satisfying the SD‑EF1 inequalities, coupled with an explicit algorithmic construction.
proof_strategy: The proof would follow a two‑step approach.  First, using a refined greedy colouring algorithm, we would show that any Δ‑bounded graph can be coloured with at most 2Δ colours while preserving an auxiliary structure that guarantees the SD‑EF1 inequalities for any common preference order.  Second, we would implement the colouring as a deterministic polynomial‑time procedure by iteratively resolving conflicts in a way that respects the strong colourability hierarchy introduced in the paper.  The key technical idea is to bound the number of recolourings needed using the fact that each vertex has at most Δ neighbours, thereby ensuring that the total running time is polynomial in |V(G)|.
title: Deterministic 2Δ-Coloring for SD-EF1 under Conflict Constraints

description:
# Future Directions: Metric Rigidity of the Petersen Graph across Valued Cayley Geometries

This cycle established that the Petersen graph — and, more generally, any graph
carrying an odd closed walk — cannot be realized isometrically inside a Cayley
graph whose generating set is the *odd part* of an integer-valued valuation on an
abelian group. The obstruction splits cleanly into a valuation-free metric core
(an isometric image pulls back proper colorings of any number of colors) and a
one-parameter certificate (the parity of the valuation two-colors the host). The
directions below push on the boundary of this dichotomy.

## Conjecture 1 (Even-valuation hosts)
There exists an abelian group `A`, an integer-valued valuation `v` all of whose
generators have **even** value, and an isometric embedding of the Petersen graph
into the associated Cayley graph.

**The key insight is** that the parity certificate is the *only* place oddness of
the valuation is used; once every generator has even value the host may contain
odd closed walks of its own, removing the coloring obstruction and potentially
opening room for a genuine isometric copy of an odd-girth graph.

**Why now?** The clean separation between the metric core and the parity
certificate isolates exactly one hypothesis to relax, turning a broad
non-embeddability statement into a sharp, testable existence question about
even-valued generating sets.

## Conjecture 2 (Valuation rank threshold)
For every abelian group `A` equipped with a valuation whose value group has rank
one, no odd-girth graph embeds isometrically into the odd-valuation Cayley graph;
but there is a rank-two valued group into which the Petersen graph does embed
isometrically.

**The key insight is** that a rank-one valuation forces a global linear order on
generator lengths, which propagates the parity obstruction along every closed
walk, whereas incomparable lengths in higher rank can cancel the length parity
that a single odd walk would otherwise force.

**Why now?** Valuation-theoretic rank is the natural graded refinement of the
present integer-valued setting, and it converts the qualitative "odd vs even"
dichotomy into a quantitative rank threshold that can be probed group by group.

## Conjecture 3 (Tropical distance spectrum)
The multiset of pairwise tropical (min-plus) path lengths realizable inside any
odd-valuation Cayley graph omits at least one distance value that the Petersen
metric requires; consequently the omission itself, not merely bipartiteness, is
the true obstruction, and it persists for a positive-density family of
non-bipartite hosts.

**The key insight is** that shortest-path distance is intrinsically a min-plus
computation, so an embedding must reproduce an entire tropical distance spectrum,
and the Petersen spectrum (diameter two, girth five) is over-determined relative
to what valuation-graded hosts can supply.

**Why now?** Recasting graph distance as a tropical eigen-quantity makes the
distance spectrum a computable invariant, so the conjectured omission can be
searched for directly across families of valued groups.

## Conjecture 4 (Universal odd-girth barrier)
Fix an odd integer `g ≥ 5`. No vertex-transitive graph of girth `g` embeds
isometrically into any odd-valuation Cayley graph, and the Petersen graph is the
smallest such witness for `g = 5`.

**The key insight is** that vertex-transitivity forces the odd closed walk to be
"spread" uniformly over the graph, so the parity obstruction cannot be localized
away by re-centering the embedding, making girth alone the controlling parameter.

**Why now?** The odd-closed-walk engine already proven here is indifferent to the
particular source graph, so extending it from Petersen to an entire girth class
is a natural and immediately checkable generalization.

## Conjecture 5 (Idempotent-coefficient rigidity)
Replacing the integer value group by an arbitrary linearly ordered idempotent
additive monoid leaves the non-embeddability intact precisely when the monoid
admits a surjection onto the two-element idempotent monoid; otherwise the barrier
disappears.

**The key insight is** that bipartiteness of the host is equivalent to the
existence of a two-valued reduction of the coefficient monoid, so the entire
obstruction is governed by the two-element quotient structure of the underlying
idempotent algebra.

**Why now?** Idempotent (tropical) coefficient systems are exactly the setting in
which distance and addition coincide, so characterizing which of them retain the
Petersen barrier pins the phenomenon to a single algebraic quotient condition.
title: That the Petersen graph — and, more generally, any graph

description:
# Future Directions — Explicit class field theory beyond the prime-degree layer

This cycle established that the smallest abelian layers over a number field — those of prime
degree — are rigid: they have cyclic Galois groups and no intermediate fields, uniformly across
the cyclotomic tower and the Hilbert class field. The following bold, falsifiable conjectures
extend that finding.

## Conjecture 1 — Lattice rigidity is exactly the "squarefree class number" phenomenon

For a number field `K`, the Hilbert class field `H/K` has a *distributive* subfield lattice that
is a Boolean-type product of prime layers precisely when the class number is squarefree; the first
non-distributive behaviour appears at the smallest square factor.

The key insight is that the subfield lattice of the class field is an exact mirror of the subgroup
lattice of the class group, so the arithmetic question "when is the tower of abelian layers
lattice-simple?" becomes the purely group-theoretic question "when is the class group a product of
distinct cyclic prime factors?" — squarefreeness of the class number.

Why now? Class numbers and class-group structures are tabulated for enormous ranges of
discriminants, so the squarefree/non-squarefree split can be tested against millions of fields
immediately, turning a structural conjecture into a data-driven one.

## Conjecture 2 — Prime-degree minimality forces a reciprocity fingerprint on splitting primes

If `H/K` is an abelian extension of prime degree `p`, then the rational primes (or prime ideals of
`K`) split completely in `H` exactly along a single congruence/ray class condition of index `p`,
and no coarser condition suffices.

The key insight is that a prime-degree layer has no room for intermediate splitting behaviour: the
absence of intermediate fields means a prime is either inert-type or fully split, so the splitting
law must be governed by one primitive character of order `p` rather than a composite of several.

Why now? The prime-degree rigidity is exactly the hypothesis under which the still-incomplete
general reciprocity law simplifies to a single character, making it the most tractable next case to
pin down explicitly and to check against known splitting tables for cubic and quintic fields.

## Conjecture 3 — Genus layers are the unique obstruction to prime-degree rigidity

The failure of subfield-lattice rigidity for a class field is controlled entirely by the 2-part
(more generally the `p`-part) of the class group: the number of independent quadratic (resp.
degree-`p`) intermediate layers equals the `p`-rank of the class group, and these are precisely the
"genus" subfields.

The key insight is that non-trivial intermediate fields can only come from non-cyclic factors of
the class group, and the count of independent minimal layers is a rank, not a size — so the entire
deviation from rigidity is measured by a single rank invariant.

Why now? `p`-ranks of class groups (especially the 2-rank via genus theory) are computable directly
from the factorization of the discriminant, so the rank-versus-layer-count identity can be verified
exhaustively for quadratic fields without computing full class groups.

## Conjecture 4 — Cyclic class groups characterize "single-generator" arithmetic

A number field has cyclic ideal class group if and only if its Hilbert class field is generated over
the base by a single algebraic element whose minimal polynomial has degree equal to the class
number — a one-parameter explicit description in the spirit of Hilbert's twelfth problem.

The key insight is that cyclicity of the class group is equivalent to cyclicity of the class-field
Galois group, and a cyclic Galois extension is exactly a simple (primitive-element) extension whose
degree is the group order, converting an abstract structural property into a concrete
single-generator statement.

Why now? Cyclic class groups dominate the statistics of small discriminants, so a single-generator
description would immediately apply to the vast majority of tabulated fields and could be checked
against explicit generators already recorded for imaginary quadratic fields of small class number.
title: That the smallest abelian layers over a number field — th
